L01 | Judgment lies in choosing an independent source that can verify the specific claim, not in waiving the check.
L02 | Judgment lies in deciding which work needs another reviewer and whose perspective is most likely to expose a blind spot.
L03 | Judgment lies in deciding how broad a claim the evidence supports, given how much evidence there is and how representative it is.
L04 | Judgment lies in choosing what to inspect at the destination to distinguish a complete result from a partial one.
L05 | Judgment lies in deciding whether a plausible source you have not searched could change the answer you give.
L06 | Judgment lies in choosing a check that can distinguish actual loss from a wrong location or a faulty reading without putting the work at risk.
L07 | Judgment lies in deciding what, if anything, the search result supports given where you looked and whether the search ran to completion.
L08 | Judgment lies in choosing a failure that represents what the test or monitor is supposed to catch.
L09 | Judgment lies in identifying the check whose result decides whether the work meets its completion criterion.
L10 | Judgment lies in identifying an observable behavior that would differ if the running program had ignored the setting.
L11 | Judgment lies in choosing a repeatable step and placing it where it can prevent the mistake.
L12 | Judgment lies in identifying what else depends on the changed part and how far the follow-up checks should extend.
L13 | Judgment lies in choosing a test that can show whether the recorded fact applies here and whether its original caveats still matter.
L14 | Judgment lies in choosing the authoritative source and the correct destination for the code, not in deciding whether to copy it by hand.
L15 | Judgment lies in choosing the time zone and precision the record needs, not in deciding whether to consult the clock.
L16 | Judgment lies in choosing words or silence that offer the calm attention the person requested without adding advice.
L17 | Judgment lies in selecting an exact passage that fairly represents the speaker and deciding whether the evidence distinguishes the proposed cause from plausible alternatives.
